## How many words at each age {#sec-findings-ds}

Children with Down syndrome understand far more words than they say, and both grow steadily across early and middle childhood. Under the model of record (VG10), a typical child is estimated to understand about `{python} words("VG10", "posterior_summary_u", 24)` words at 24 months, `{python} words("VG10", "posterior_summary_u", 36)` at 36 months, `{python} words("VG10", "posterior_summary_u", 60)` at 60 months, and `{python} words("VG10", "posterior_summary_u", 90)` by 90 months (out of the 800-word reference inventory; @sec-betabinomial). Spoken vocabulary lags well behind: about `{python} words("VG10", "posterior_summary_s", 24)` words at 24 months, `{python} words("VG10", "posterior_summary_s", 36)` at 36 months, and `{python} words("VG10", "posterior_summary_s", 60)` at 60 months.

@fig-ds-joint shows both trajectories with their uncertainty bands. The estimates here are for the *typical* child (posterior median with a 94% credible interval); the wider bands for individual children are tabulated in @sec-reference-tables.

![Expected words understood and spoken by age, children with Down syndrome (VG10), with 50% and 94% highest-density intervals.](figures/VG10-age-understood-spoken-ds-re-subj-uq-anchored/joint_trajectory_hdi.svg){#fig-ds-joint .lightbox fig-align="left"}

::: {.callout-tip}
The full age-by-age tables — expected counts for a typical child *and* the range across individual children — are in @sec-reference-tables. The univariate models VG01 (spoken) and VG02 (understood) give closely agreeing cross-checks (Appendix B1).
:::

## How fast children learn

The rate of word learning is not constant: it accelerates through the preschool years as vocabulary builds. @fig-ds-rate-u and @fig-ds-rate-s show the expected number of new words gained per month for understanding and speaking. Comprehension growth peaks earlier; spoken-word growth accelerates later, once production gets underway (see the production ratio below).

![Expected rate of learning words understood (words/month) by age (VG10).](figures/VG10-age-understood-spoken-ds-re-subj-uq-anchored/expected_learning_rate_u.svg){#fig-ds-rate-u .lightbox fig-align="left"}

![Expected rate of learning words spoken (words/month) by age (VG10).](figures/VG10-age-understood-spoken-ds-re-subj-uq-anchored/expected_learning_rate_s.svg){#fig-ds-rate-s .lightbox fig-align="left"}

## Understanding versus saying: the comprehension–production gap

A central feature of vocabulary development in Down syndrome is that understanding runs ahead of production. The **production ratio** $q(a) = P(\text{speak} \mid \text{understood})$ (@sec-ratios) captures the fraction of understood words a child also says. Under VG10 it rises from about `{python} f'{val("VG10","posterior_summary_q",24,"q_median")*100:.0f}'`% at 24 months to about `{python} f'{val("VG10","posterior_summary_q",48,"q_median")*100:.0f}'`% at 48 months and around `{python} f'{val("VG10","posterior_summary_q",72,"q_median")*100:.0f}'`% by 72 months, after which it plateaus — children come to say most, but not all, of the words they understand.

![The production ratio $q(a)$ — the fraction of understood words that are spoken — by age (VG10).](figures/VG10-age-understood-spoken-ds-re-subj-uq-anchored/production_rate.svg){#fig-ds-q .lightbox fig-align="left"}

Expressed as counts, the **gap** between words understood and words spoken widens through the preschool years — reaching roughly `{python} f'{round(val("VG10","comprehension_production_gap",37,"gap_median")):d}'` words around `{python} "37"` months — and then narrows as production catches up (@fig-ds-gap).

![The comprehension–production gap (expected words understood minus spoken) by age (VG10).](figures/VG10-age-understood-spoken-ds-re-subj-uq-anchored/comprehension_production_gap.svg){#fig-ds-gap .lightbox fig-align="left"}

## How much children differ

Variability between children is large and grows with age. The model captures this in two ways: age-varying dispersion $\kappa(z)$ (@sec-kappa), which widens the spread of counts at older ages, and subject random effects (@sec-randomeffects), which allow each child their own level. @fig-ds-spread shows the resulting distribution of spoken-word counts by age — the range across individual children is much wider than the uncertainty in the typical trajectory, which is why the practical reference (@sec-reference-tables) reports both.

![Posterior predictive distribution of words spoken by age, children with Down syndrome (VG10).](figures/VG10-age-understood-spoken-ds-re-subj-uq-anchored/posterior_predictive_count_distributions_s.svg){#fig-ds-spread .lightbox fig-align="left"}
